faq.question: Is a retry a second underwriting?
faq.answer: A retry of the same authorized run does not create a second underwriting charge. A new full underwriting is a distinct authorized request.

label: Our manifesto
title: Risk is a movie.
description: We believe financial decisions deserve the context of a changing financial life—not just the snapshot that was easiest to collect.

sections.title: 01 / Connect what was separate.
sections.body: A transaction belongs to an account. An account belongs to an entity. An entity has relationships, obligations, and a history. Intelligence starts when we can see those connections and trace the evidence behind them.

sections.title: 02 / Keep uncertainty visible.
sections.body: A confident-looking number cannot replace missing context. Coverage, freshness, conflicting evidence, and unresolved questions should be part of an assessment, not footnotes that disappear.

sections.title: 03 / Follow the change.
sections.body: The moment capital moves is not the moment risk stops. A borrower’s circumstances continue to evolve. The intelligence supporting that relationship should evolve with them.

sections.title: 04 / Make the reasoning reviewable.
sections.body: An institution needs to understand why a signal appeared and which evidence supports it. Useful intelligence helps a person ask a better question and take responsibility for the answer.

sections.title: 05 / Keep the institution in control.
sections.body: Technology should strengthen the team that owns the customer relationship. Policy, approval, communication, and intervention belong with the institution—not with an unexplained black box.

label: Perspective · Monitoring
title: From a snapshot
description: Why monitoring begins with a clear account of what was known at underwriting.

sections.title: A baseline is a set of assumptions, not just a score.
sections.body: An underwriting captures a view of income, obligations, liquidity, and the information available at a particular time. If those inputs change, the original conclusion may deserve a second look. Keeping the baseline means preserving the evidence and assumptions that made the assessment meaningful.

sections.title: Compare like with like.
sections.body: A drop in observed deposits can have several explanations. A business may be seasonal, a connection may have stopped refreshing, or trading conditions may have changed. A useful signal helps the reviewer distinguish those possibilities by showing coverage and timing alongside the observation.

sections.title: Make the review actionable.
sections.body: A monitoring workflow should tell a team what changed, where to look, and who owns the next step. It does not need to decide every action automatically. For many institutions, the most valuable result is a precise, evidence-backed reason to review a borrower.

sections.title: Close the loop with the institution.
sections.body: AMLOK Signal supplies results, alerts, and evidence. The institution decides whether to request more information, adjust an exposure, or continue monitoring. That separation keeps the customer relationship and final decision with the team responsible for them.

label: Perspective · Financial evidence
title: Read the cash flow.
description: Why a deposit is a starting point for analysis, rather than the answer to an income question.

sections.title: The balance alone cannot explain the business.
sections.body: A bank account reflects operating receipts, transfers, borrowing, refunds, and other activity. Combining those movements into one total can obscure the financial pattern an analyst is trying to understand. Classification matters because different flows have different implications for capacity.

sections.title: Bring another source into the conversation.
sections.body: Payment-platform records can help explain receipts. Accounting data can offer a view of invoices and expenses. A statement can show settlement timing. These sources are useful together when their periods, identifiers, and coverage are understood; one should not silently be treated as a substitute for another.

sections.title: Keep the exceptions.
sections.body: Unreconciled movements and incomplete history are information. An assessment that makes those gaps visible gives the institution an opportunity to request evidence or constrain a conclusion. Filling them with an assumption creates apparent precision without a stronger foundation.

sections.title: Read the pattern over time.
sections.body: A borrower’s capacity is not defined by one good month. Examining volatility, obligations, and recurring patterns helps turn financial activity into a question a credit team can evaluate. The institution’s policy determines how that evidence affects its decision.

label: Perspective · Decision design
title: Build intelligence
description: Evidence, uncertainty, and human ownership are design requirements for a useful risk workflow.

sections.title: An explanation needs somewhere to go.
sections.body: A summary is more useful when a reviewer can follow it back to supporting records. Evidence lineage connects a statement to the source and time window it describes. It lets the reviewer check the interpretation rather than accept the wording on trust.

sections.title: Make uncertainty part of the interface.
sections.body: Missing periods, conflicting records, and limited coverage should be legible where the assessment is reviewed. The goal is not to make every output appear certain. It is to help the team understand which conclusions have support and which need more information.

sections.title: Keep policy ownership explicit.
sections.body: The organization taking the credit risk sets its policy and owns its final decisions. A workflow should make review gates, exception handling, and the handoff to institution systems clear. Those boundaries help an assessment become operationally useful.

sections.title: Evaluate the whole workflow.
sections.body: A convincing demonstration is only one part of validation. Teams also need to understand how the system handles incomplete evidence, repeated events, unavailable sources, and unexpected changes. Designing those paths carefully is part of designing the product itself.

label: Webhooks

sections.title: Subscribe to meaningful changes

sections.title: Verify, persist, then acknowledge
sections.body: Validate the signature against the exact request bytes. Accept events into a durable inbox before returning success, and process them asynchronously with workspace-aware deduplication.

label: Site map
title: Find your way.
description: Explore every page across the AMLOK platform, products, industries, developer resources, and company.

label: Connected data
title: See the connections.
description: Why the connections between borrowers, accounts, and obligations matter as much as the records themselves.

sections.title: Start with the relationship, not the score.
sections.body: A borrower rarely fits inside one record. A business can hold several bank accounts, collect payments through different processors, and share ownership with other entities. Looking at each source separately can leave a reviewer with individually accurate facts and an incomplete picture. A connected risk graph provides a way to organise those facts around the relationships that make them meaningful.

sections.title: Keep the evidence attached.
sections.body: A useful connection should answer three questions: what relates these records, which source supports that relationship, and when was it observed? A verified ownership relationship is different from a similar name or a shared address. Preserve that distinction. Keep uncertain matches available for review instead of turning them into established facts. The graph should make the evidence easier to inspect, including the reasons a connection may be incomplete.

sections.title: Read movement in context.
sections.body: Consider a transfer between two accounts held by the same business. Without the relationship, the deposit could be counted as fresh revenue. With the relationship and transaction evidence in view, a reviewer can distinguish movement inside the business from new receipts. The same principle applies to obligations, related entities, and recurring flows. Context changes the questions a team asks; it does not remove the need to check the underlying record.

sections.title: Build a graph that can change.
sections.body: An ownership record, an account connection, and a transaction history do not refresh on the same schedule. A practical graph needs dates, source coverage, and a clear treatment of missing data. New evidence may strengthen a relationship, challenge it, or show that it is no longer current. Keeping that history makes it possible to explain why the present view differs from the one used at underwriting.

sections.title: Keep judgment with the institution.
sections.body: The goal is a more reviewable picture of risk. AMLOK connects financial evidence and borrower context so a team can investigate relationships across the credit lifecycle. Lending policy, exceptions, and final decisions remain with the institution. A graph is most useful when it helps that team ask a better question and trace the answer back to evidence.

label: Monitoring
title: Less noise.
description: Design monitoring around meaningful changes, clear evidence, and a team that knows what happens next.

sections.title: Begin with a reviewable question.
sections.body: An alert is only useful if someone can explain why it deserves attention. “Revenue moved” is a starting point. “Receipts changed relative to a comparable period, with these records supporting the change” gives a reviewer something to investigate. Define the question before choosing a threshold, and connect it to the institution’s policy and review process.

sections.title: Separate a change in risk from a change in coverage.
sections.body: A disconnected account can resemble a sudden decline in activity. A delayed data feed can make an otherwise stable borrower look different. Monitoring should carry freshness and coverage alongside the observation. Teams need to know whether they are seeing a change in the borrower’s financial behaviour or a change in the information available to them.

sections.title: Make the baseline explicit.
sections.body: A meaningful comparison needs a stated window and a reason that window is appropriate. Seasonal businesses, recent borrowers, and businesses with uneven billing cycles require different context. Preserve the baseline established during underwriting, then explain how later observations relate to it. Avoid silently changing the comparison while presenting the result as if it were continuous.

sections.title: Design the handoff.
sections.body: Attach the supporting evidence, the affected borrower, and the reason for the signal. Define which team reviews it and which system records the outcome. Repeated signals may belong to the same underlying change; grouping them can make the review clearer. AMLOK Signal supplies monitoring intelligence, while the institution owns borrower communication, case handling, and any resulting action.

label: Cash flow
title: Merchant receipts need
description: A practical perspective on sales, settlements, refunds, and the timing behind merchant cash flow.

sections.title: Sales and settlements tell different stories.
sections.body: A sale recorded by a commerce platform is not always a deposit received by a bank account on the same day. Settlement timing, fees, refunds, and reserves can change both the amount and the date. Reading only one side can leave a funding team with a misleading sense of the money available to the business.

sections.title: Connect the observation windows.
sections.body: When comparing processor activity with banking evidence, start by checking that the periods overlap. State which accounts and channels are covered. A merchant may use more than one processor or move receipts between accounts. Differences should lead to reconciliation questions rather than automatic conclusions about missing revenue.

sections.title: Look beyond the strongest week.
sections.body: Recurring obligations, changing sales concentration, and irregular receipts matter alongside total volume. A strong trading period may coincide with a large upcoming payment or an unusual promotion. A useful review considers the pattern and its limits, instead of treating one peak period as a stable operating baseline.

sections.title: Keep the funding decision separate from the evidence.
sections.body: Connected financial information can help a team understand the merchant and follow later changes. It does not set the institution’s terms or replace its policy. AMLOK’s cash-flow intelligence is designed to preserve the context and source evidence around financial activity so reviewers can make and revisit their own decisions.

label: Underwriting
title: The decision is a moment.
description: Carry the assumptions behind underwriting into the monitoring that follows funding.

sections.title: Write down what the decision depended on.
sections.body: An underwriting decision is built on a view of the borrower at a particular time. The evidence window, obligations, recurring receipts, and policy exceptions are part of that view. If those assumptions disappear after funding, monitoring starts without a clear account of what it is trying to follow.

sections.title: Define the handoff before funding.
sections.body: A useful handoff identifies the borrower, the authorised sources, the observation window, and the questions that remain open. It also names the team responsible for reviewing a later change. This is a shared context, not a second approval process. The institution’s policies determine what should be followed and which conditions need further review.

sections.title: Compare new evidence to the original context.
sections.body: A later observation becomes more useful when it can be traced to the baseline. Did recurring receipts change? Is an obligation still visible? Has source coverage become incomplete? Explain both the new observation and the quality of the comparison. A difference between two snapshots is not automatically a change in creditworthiness.

sections.title: Make continuity part of the design.
sections.body: AMLOK Insights supports underwriting intelligence, and Signal supports monitoring after origination. Connecting them around borrower evidence helps teams retain context across the lifecycle. The institution remains responsible for lending policy, the decision to fund, and any subsequent servicing or collections action.

label: AI & workflows
title: Every event needs
description: How to design evidence-led automation without losing ownership, review, or the history of a decision.

sections.title: Distinguish an event from an instruction.
sections.body: A new document, a refreshed account, or a changed observation tells a system that something happened. It does not, by itself, authorise a borrower-facing action. Keep the event, the policy evaluation, and the resulting task separate so a reviewer can understand the path from evidence to action.

sections.title: Plan for the ordinary failure modes.
sections.body: Events can arrive more than once or in an unexpected order. A downstream system may be temporarily unavailable. Workflows should retain identifiers, recognise already-processed events, and make retries visible. The goal is predictable handling, including when a workflow cannot safely continue.

sections.title: Make review a first-class step.
sections.body: Not every situation should be resolved by automation. Incomplete evidence, conflicting records, and an unfamiliar exception may need a person to assess the context. Give that reviewer the source record, the relevant policy, and a clear explanation of what is uncertain. A queue entry without evidence simply moves the investigation elsewhere.

sections.title: Measure the whole handoff.
sections.body: A completed workflow is more than a successful API response. Consider whether the intended system received the information, whether the review had an owner, and whether the outcome can be traced. AMLOK intelligence can support the workflow; the institution’s systems and teams remain responsible for the operational actions it authorises.

label: Embedded finance
title: One connection.
description: What an embedded financial-data experience should preserve beyond the initial connection.

sections.title: Make the request understandable.
sections.body: A connection experience should help a borrower understand which source they are connecting and why it is relevant. Banking, accounting, commerce, and payment records serve different purposes. Present the options clearly, and keep the institution’s approved disclosures and consent process close to the step where access is requested.

sections.title: Respect the differences between sources.
sections.body: An accounting record, a card settlement, and a bank transaction describe different parts of the same activity. They may use different dates, identifiers, and reporting periods. A shared interface should not flatten those differences. Carry the source, time window, and available coverage into the resulting review.

sections.title: Design for interruption.
sections.body: A borrower may leave midway through the flow, choose the wrong institution, or encounter a connection that needs attention. Explain the current state and provide a clear recovery path. Avoid presenting a partial connection as a complete financial picture. The reviewer should see what arrived and what is still missing.

sections.title: Connect the experience to the lifecycle.
sections.body: An embedded experience is the beginning of a relationship with evidence. The institution needs to understand the access scope, refresh behaviour, and handling of a later disconnection. AMLOK supports branded connection experiences and connected risk intelligence, while the institution controls the borrower relationship and its policy decisions.
